\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs.
As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data \cite{shumailov2024_nature,alemohammad2024_mad}.
This model$\to$data$\to$model cycle is no longer hypothetical---it is already occurring in the wild---yet we lack the ability to determine how many recursive iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality \cite{dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails}.

Existing tools address adjacent but distinct problems.
Binary detectors such as Binoculars \cite{binoculars2024}, Fast-DetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt2024}, and DivEye \cite{diveye2026} classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths $d \geq 1$ into a single category.
Watermarking \cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively.
The model collapse literature \cite{shumailov2024_nature,dohmatob2024_tale_of_tails} assumes depth is known a priori; \citet{drayson2025_detection_prevents_collapse} filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths.
No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are consistent across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied.
Specifically, perplexity tail statistics---the 90th-percentile perplexity (\textsc{p90\_ppl}) and surprisal variance (\textsc{var\_surprisal})---emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 8/9 model--strategy configurations, respectively.

We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it.
Given a text passage, we compute a feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics---19 candidates capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity, though high multicollinearity concentrates the signal in ${\approx}$4--5 effective dimensions (\S\ref{sec:atlas:features})---and classify it with a Random Forest into one of $K{+}1$ depth classes ($d{=}0$ for human text through $d{=}K$ for $K$-th generation text).
To systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas}: a $3 \times 3$ grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus $p{=}0.95$, temperature $\tau{=}0.9$, top-$k$ $k{=}50$), each spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples.
The atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories---temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-$k$ attenuates the depth signal---and we introduce the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Task formalization.} We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification and introduce the EDD metric, which summarizes the maximum depth at which adjacent generations remain separable above a given AUC threshold.

    \item \textbf{Depth Degradation Atlas.} We construct a systematic $3 \times 3$ map across model families and decoding strategies, revealing that \textsc{p90\_ppl} ranks in the top 2 in all 9 cells and \textsc{var\_surprisal} in 8/9, with a mean Spearman rank correlation of $\rho{=}0.868$ across importance vectors. The extended Pythia nucleus pipeline (d0--d5) yields $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$, establishing that depth discrimination persists through four recursive steps before falling below threshold.

    \item \textbf{Generalization analysis.} Cross-model leave-one-out transfer achieves 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\% (chance = 25\%). We decompose a temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion into a scale component---partially correctable by per-strategy normalization---and a residual structural component that simple normalization cannot resolve.

    \item \textbf{End-to-end learning.} Both DeBERTa-v3-base (58.3\%) and RoBERTa-base (59.5\%) achieve ${\sim}$59\% via end-to-end finetuning---19pp below feature-based classifiers (78.2\%)---with the architecture-invariant gap ruling out model selection bias. Linear probing confirms that PLM representations cannot recover perplexity tail features (negative $R^2$), while SHAP analysis shows these features account for 88.8\% of RF's contribution.
\end{itemize}

\begin{abstract}
As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model$\to$data$\to$model loop arises---yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone.
We formalize \emph{recursive generation depth estimation} as ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths.
From each passage we extract a compact statistical fingerprint---19 candidate features dominated by perplexity tail statistics, with the top 5 achieving 97.6\% of full-set performance---computed against a fixed reference model (GPT-2 base, 124M).
A Random Forest classifier achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy (chance = 25\%; 58.8--82.6\% when excluding the near-perfectly separable d0 class; a zero-shot LLM baseline reaches only 36.2\%), with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as consistent depth markers across the studied $3 \times 3$ grid (top-2 importance in 9/9 and 8/9 cells, respectively).
Our \emph{Depth Degradation Atlas} reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories rather than merely attenuating them, and we define the \emph{Effective Discriminable Depth} (EDD) metric, finding $\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ for extended recursion chains.
Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4\% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1\%; temperature sampling induces a d1/d2 AUC inversion that we decompose into a correctable scale component and a residual structural component.
Applied to WikiText-103 (546 passages), all three model-specific classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy despite $+$621\% domain shift in mean perplexity; on C4 web-crawl text, false positive rates range from 4.7\% to 22.4\%, concentrated in template content.
\end{abstract}

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Cross-strategy deployment constraint.}
Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling.
Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inversion (GPT-2~XL d1v2 AUC $0.24{\to}0.56$, OLMo $0.19{\to}0.70$) but leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (${\sim}0.83$), indicating that a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification + strategy-conditioned classification) is needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.

\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}
Depth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$98\% across all nine model--strategy settings), inflating headline accuracy.
Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).

\paragraph{Controlled vs.\ ecological setting.}
All experiments use Wikipedia seed text with controlled recursive generation (LoRA fine-tuning, 1--1.5B parameter models).
This protocol isolates the recursive depth variable but diverges from wild recursive contamination, where models are pretrained on mixed corpora containing prior-generation outputs at unknown proportions; the fingerprints we identify may attenuate or shift under such diffuse exposure.
Depth signal is the dominant classification factor (5-fold CV 59--82\%, up to 2.5$\times$ chance): LOGO accuracy (72.1\%) matches standard CV (72.0\%), and seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\% vs.\ 10\%; Appendix~\ref{app:domain_bias}).
Transfer to instruction-tuned models and larger scales (7B+) remains open.
Real-world documents may also interleave segments at different recursive generation depths; extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity--statistical-power tradeoff.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent false positive rate.}
On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5{,}000 passages), FPR ranges from 4.7\% (OLMo) to 22.4\% (GPT-2~XL).
Misclassifications concentrate in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (\texttt{rep\_3gram} $+$37\%, \texttt{rep\_4gram} $+$75\% vs.\ correctly classified d0); the model gap likely reflects training data composition (OLMo's Dolma includes diverse web data vs.\ Pythia/GPT-2~XL's Wikipedia/WebText).
Deployment on heterogeneous web corpora requires model- and domain-specific calibration.

\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
Adversarial paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.

\paragraph{EDD monotonicity assumption.}
Our EDD definition (Eq.~\ref{eq:edd}) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth $d^*$ to exceed $T$, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically---as observed in all our configurations.
However, \citet{bakshi2026_collapse_improvement} show that early recursion can temporarily \emph{improve} model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d2/d3).
Our cross-strategy transfer results provide an empirical example: training on nucleus + top-$k$ and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2~XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption.
In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work.
The choice of threshold $T$ is also application-dependent: at $T{=}0.80$, several cells lose one depth level relative to $T{=}0.75$.

\paragraph{Reference model dependency.}
Surprisal-based features are computed relative to GPT-2 base (124M), introducing partial overlap when GPT-2~XL is held out, though GPT-2~XL holdout accuracy (67.6\%) does not exceed the unrelated OLMo (69.2\%).
The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.

\paragraph{Additional caveats.}
Detection features degrade under domain shift \cite{pudasaini2026_detection_fails}; our depth features are likely susceptible.
\citet{falahati2026_curated} show that curated synthetic data need not trigger collapse, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2~XL) and Wikipedia text as seed data.
No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released.
Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.
Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

\paragraph{d0 inflation of headline metrics.}
Depth~0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall $>$98\% across all nine model--strategy settings), inflating headline accuracy.
Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4\% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8\% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).

\paragraph{Controlled vs.\ ecological setting.}
All experiments use Wikipedia seed text with controlled recursive generation (LoRA fine-tuning, 1--1.5B parameter models).
This protocol isolates the recursive depth variable but diverges from wild recursive contamination, where models are pretrained on mixed corpora containing prior-generation outputs at unknown proportions; the fingerprints we identify may attenuate or shift under such diffuse exposure.
Depth signal is the dominant classification factor (5-fold CV 59--82\%, up to 2.5$\times$ chance): LOGO accuracy (72.1\%) matches standard CV (72.0\%), and seed-group prediction is at chance (10.2\% vs.\ 10\%; Appendix~\ref{app:domain_bias}).
Transfer to instruction-tuned models and larger scales (7B+) remains open.
Real-world documents may also interleave segments at different recursive generation depths; extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity--statistical-power tradeoff.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent false positive rate.}
On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve $\geq$98.5\% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5{,}000 passages), FPR ranges from 4.7\% (OLMo) to 22.4\% (GPT-2~XL).
Misclassifications concentrate in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (\texttt{rep\_3gram} $+$37\%, \texttt{rep\_4gram} $+$75\% vs.\ correctly classified d0); the model gap likely reflects training data composition (OLMo's Dolma includes diverse web data vs.\ Pythia/GPT-2~XL's Wikipedia/WebText).
Deployment on heterogeneous web corpora requires model- and domain-specific calibration.

\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
Adversarial paraphrasing \cite{sadasivan2023_paraphrase} could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.

1	\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that a compact feature set dominated by perplexity tail statistics achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ across models; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}), with five features sufficing for 97.6\% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within $\leq$0.4pp.
5	The dominant pair (\texttt{p90\_ppl} top-2 in 9/9 cells, \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 under SHAP) generalizes across the three studied model families without retraining, making depth estimation a candidate early-warning signal for model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024_nature} within this experimental scope.
6	Recent work corroborates this connection, identifying entropy decline as a measurable signal of recursive degradation that parallels the tail erosion our features capture~\cite{shi2025_closer_look}.
7	
8	Cross-strategy transfer remains the primary bottleneck (59.1\% vs.\ 66.4\% cross-model), with the temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion making single-classifier deployment across unknown decoding strategies infeasible.
9	A two-stage pipeline---first identifying the decoding strategy, then applying a strategy-conditioned depth classifier---could address this, though automating strategy identification from text alone requires independent validation.
10	
11	\paragraph{Depth-graduated data curation.}
12	Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction~\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
13	Depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) whose distributional properties remain close to the human source, while down-weighting or filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.
14	As a proof of concept, we fine-tune Pythia-410M with LoRA ($r{=}16$) for 3 epochs on subsets selected by RF-predicted depth, random subsampling, or oracle depth labels (8 conditions, 5 seeds each; Table~\ref{tab:curation_poc}).
15	RF depth-based filtering significantly outperforms size-matched random subsampling at all three stringency tiers (strict 25\%: $\Delta{=}0.43$ PPL, $p{=}0.002$; moderate 50\%: $\Delta{=}0.24$, $p{=}0.02$; soft 44\%: $\Delta{=}0.33$, $p{<}0.001$; paired $t$-tests), and the soft-threshold RF condition achieves perplexity statistically indistinguishable from unfiltered training on the full 10{,}000 samples while using only 44\% of the data ($p{=}0.41$).
16	Interestingly, oracle-strict filtering does not improve over unfiltered ($p{=}0.22$), suggesting that classifier imprecision preserves beneficial data diversity that pure depth thresholding removes.
17	Importance weighting~\cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting} could further enable continuous depth-aware data selection rather than discrete thresholding, and verification-guided retraining offers a complementary mitigation path~\cite{yi2026_escaping_collapse}.
18	Full per-condition statistics appear in Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}.
19	
20	\paragraph{Toward a provenance toolkit.}
21	Depth estimation complements existing provenance methods along orthogonal axes.
22	Watermarking~\cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} provides high-confidence attribution when the generator cooperates but is inapplicable to unwatermarked text.
23	Source attribution~\cite{uchendu2020_attribution} identifies the generating model but not the generation history.
24	Bevendorff et al.\ distinguish attribution from verification as two fundamental detection paradigms~\cite{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms}; depth estimation represents a complementary third axis that characterizes \emph{iterative reuse} regardless of generator cooperation or identity.
25	A layered provenance system combining watermark presence, source model, and recursive depth could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.
26	
27	\paragraph{Mixed-depth documents.}

\section{Discussion and Conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}

We formalized recursive generation depth estimation and showed that a compact feature set dominated by perplexity tail statistics achieves 70--85\% four-class accuracy ($\mathrm{EDD}_{0.75}{=}4$ across models; \S\ref{sec:atlas:edd}), with five features sufficing for 97.6\% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within $\leq$0.4pp.
The dominant pair (\texttt{p90\_ppl} top-2 in 9/9 cells, \texttt{var\_surprisal} in 8/9 under SHAP) generalizes across the three studied model families without retraining, making depth estimation a candidate early-warning signal for model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024_nature} within this experimental scope.
Recent work corroborates this connection, identifying entropy decline as a measurable signal of recursive degradation that parallels the tail erosion our features capture~\cite{shi2025_closer_look}.

Cross-strategy transfer remains the primary bottleneck (59.1\% vs.\ 66.4\% cross-model), with the temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion making single-classifier deployment across unknown decoding strategies infeasible.
A two-stage pipeline---first identifying the decoding strategy, then applying a strategy-conditioned depth classifier---could address this, though automating strategy identification from text alone requires independent validation.

\paragraph{Depth-graduated data curation.}
Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction~\cite{dsir2023,qurating2024}.
Depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) whose distributional properties remain close to the human source, while down-weighting or filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality.
As a proof of concept, we fine-tune Pythia-410M with LoRA ($r{=}16$) for 3 epochs on subsets selected by RF-predicted depth, random subsampling, or oracle depth labels (8 conditions, 5 seeds each; Table~\ref{tab:curation_poc}).
RF depth-based filtering significantly outperforms size-matched random subsampling at all three stringency tiers (strict 25\%: $\Delta{=}0.43$ PPL, $p{=}0.002$; moderate 50\%: $\Delta{=}0.24$, $p{=}0.02$; soft 44\%: $\Delta{=}0.33$, $p{<}0.001$; paired $t$-tests), and the soft-threshold RF condition achieves perplexity statistically indistinguishable from unfiltered training on the full 10{,}000 samples while using only 44\% of the data ($p{=}0.41$).
Interestingly, oracle-strict filtering does not improve over unfiltered ($p{=}0.22$), suggesting that classifier imprecision preserves beneficial data diversity that pure depth thresholding removes.
Importance weighting~\cite{sugiyama2007_importance_weighting} could further enable continuous depth-aware data selection rather than discrete thresholding, and verification-guided retraining offers a complementary mitigation path~\cite{yi2026_escaping_collapse}.
Full per-condition statistics appear in Appendix~\ref{app:curation_poc}.

\paragraph{Toward a provenance toolkit.}
Depth estimation complements existing provenance methods along orthogonal axes.
Watermarking~\cite{kirchenbauer2023_watermark} provides high-confidence attribution when the generator cooperates but is inapplicable to unwatermarked text.
Source attribution~\cite{uchendu2020_attribution} identifies the generating model but not the generation history.
Bevendorff et al.\ distinguish attribution from verification as two fundamental detection paradigms~\cite{bevendorff2025_two_paradigms}; depth estimation represents a complementary third axis that characterizes \emph{iterative reuse} regardless of generator cooperation or identity.
A layered provenance system combining watermark presence, source model, and recursive depth could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.

\paragraph{Mixed-depth documents.}
Real-world corpora often interleave segments at different recursive depths within a single document.
Sliding-window depth estimation at the segment level offers a natural extension: windows of 256--512 tokens preserve sufficient statistical power for tail feature computation while enabling sub-document depth maps.
Such maps could inform paragraph-level data curation, selectively retaining low-depth segments even from partially contaminated documents, and would complement document-level classifiers that flag mixed-provenance content for manual review.

\paragraph{Adversarial robustness.}
Adversarial post-processing---paraphrasing, back-translation, or targeted lexical substitution---poses a natural threat to depth estimation.
Because perplexity tail statistics reflect distributional properties of the recursive generation process rather than surface lexical patterns, they exhibit inherent resistance to shallow transformations that preserve the underlying surprisal structure.
However, robustness to targeted attacks that explicitly optimize the output perplexity distribution---e.g., iterative rewriting guided by tail-statistic objectives---remains unverified, and attack-aware features (syntactic complexity, discourse coherence markers) may be necessary for deployment in adversarial settings.

\paragraph{Scaling predictions.}
All current experiments use 1--1.5B parameter models; larger models (7B+) generate more fluent text with narrower perplexity distributions, potentially compressing inter-depth separability.
However, recursive training amplifies distributional artifacts regardless of base model quality: tail erosion is driven by retraining on one's own output distribution, not by model capacity per se.
We therefore expect depth estimation to remain feasible at larger scales, though recalibration of feature thresholds and possibly richer feature sets (e.g., attention entropy or generation diversity metrics) will likely be required.

\paragraph{Limitations and future directions.}
Real-world documents may interleave passages at mixed recursive depths within a single document; our passage-level classifier assumes uniform depth, and extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity--statistical-power tradeoff that remains unexplored.
Web-crawl deployment requires model-specific calibration (C4 FPR: 4.7--22.4\%; Table~\ref{tab:calibration}), and all experiments use 1--1.5B models.
Adversarial robustness is only partially characterized: tail-based features resist surface-level paraphrasing due to their dependence on deep distributional structure, but targeted distribution-aware attacks remain untested.
Future work should validate on mixed-domain corpora at larger scales and evaluate whether depth-graduated curation, with appropriate strategy conditioning, improves downstream training outcomes.
